# Payment Gateway Fraud Detection

End-to-end take-home: EDA → point-in-time features → Logistic Regression baseline + XGBoost →
time-based evaluation → release checks → drift monitoring on "live" Jul–Sep traffic.

## Data used (please read)

* `data/fraud_detection_sample_transactions.csv` — the provided 12-row sample (4 frauds, 33% fraud rate).
  It only demonstrates the schema and is far too small to train on.
* `data/transactions_synthetic.csv` — **synthetic** data generated by `src/generate_data.py`
  (seed 42, fully reproducible), same schema, 1 Jan – 30 Sep 2026, ~1.2% fraud in Jan–Jun.
  The 12 sample rows are included as the first rows. Public datasets (e.g. the Kaggle credit-card
  PCA set) don't have MCC/device/service_type fields, so a simulator was the only way to exercise
  every requested feature and drift scenario.

The simulator injects known fraud patterns (test-then-spike bursts from one device, late-night
high-value txns at high-risk merchants, account-takeover-style amounts) and, in Jul–Sep, deliberate
changes: wallet growth, a **new fraud pattern** (mid-value UPI fraud at newly onboarded merchants
in MCC 4829/5816) and a **data-quality incident** (some wallet amounts arrive in paise from mid-Sep).
**All results below are on synthetic data; they show the method, not real-world performance.**

## Setup & run

```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
bash run_all.sh          # ~3-4 min: generate -> EDA -> train -> release checks -> monitor -> tests
```

Individual steps: `python src/generate_data.py | eda.py | train.py | validate.py | monitor.py`, `python -m pytest -q`.

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `src/generate_data.py` | synthetic data simulator |
| `src/eda.py` | EDA → `reports/eda.md` |
| `src/features.py` | point-in-time feature engineering (batch + online versions) |
| `src/train.py` | LR + XGBoost, imbalance comparison, thresholds, bootstrap CIs → `reports/model_results.md`, `artifacts/` |
| `src/validate.py` | pre-release checks → `reports/release_checks.md` |
| `src/monitor.py` | data / prediction / performance / business monitoring → `reports/monitoring_report.md` |
| `tests/` | leakage, training-serving parity and schema-validation tests |

## 1. Data understanding (`reports/eda.md`)

Jan–Jun: **87,531 transactions, 1,063 frauds, fraud rate 1.21%**. Predicting "all genuine" would be
98.8% accurate, so accuracy is not used.

| Signal | Fraud rate |
|---|---|
| Night (00–05h) vs rest | 17.9% vs ~0.4% |
| Merchant tier high / medium / low | 11.9% / 2.1% / 0.25% |
| MCC: gambling, money transfer, prepaid card load | 16% / 11% / 10.5% |
| Amount > ₹20k vs < ₹1k | ~8.7% vs 0.3% |
| ≥2 prior txns from same device in 10 min | 23.5% vs 0.8% |
| Brand-new device | 3.8% vs 1.0% |
| Wallet vs UPI | 2.4% vs 0.8% |
| Status FAILED/DECLINED vs SUCCESS | ~7% vs 0.8% (**not used**, see below) |

**Fields not used directly, and what is derived instead**

| Field | Why not raw | Derived features |
|---|---|---|
| `request_id` | unique ID, no signal | none |
| `device_id` | ID / quasi-PII, high cardinality | device txn counts in 10m/1h/24h/30d, amount sum 1h, seconds since last txn, device age, is-new, amount vs device's prior mean, prior failures in 24h, has device seen this merchant |
| `merchant_id` | high-cardinality ID | merchant age, counts 1h/7d, amount vs merchant's prior mean |
| `request_time` | raw timestamp doesn't generalise | hour, day of week, night, weekend |
| `request_status` | **leakage**: known only after processing, often the output of an existing fraud rule | only *past* failures of the device (`dev_fail_cnt_24h`) |
| `mcc_title` | duplicate of `mcc_code` | — |
| `merchant_city` | redundant with state, sparse | (state used) |
| `currency_code` | constant (INR) | validated, not modelled |
| `fraud_label` of past txns | labels arrive weeks later (chargebacks) | never used as a feature (no target encoding of merchant/device fraud history) |

## 2. Model

* **Features** (28): time, amount (log, round ₹1000, ends in 999), the device/merchant behaviour above,
  plus categoricals `service_type, merchant_type, mcc_code, issuer_bank, merchant_state`.
  Every behavioural feature is **point-in-time** (uses only strictly earlier events). Rolling windows and ages
  capped at 30 days are used instead of lifetime counters, which grow with calendar time and drift by construction.
* **Missing values**: categoricals → explicit `MISSING` level; `NOT_APPLICABLE` issuer for wallets kept as its own
  level. LR uses median imputation + missing indicators; XGBoost uses native NaN handling. Unseen/rare
  categories → one-hot "infrequent" bucket.
* **Time-based split**: January = feature warm-up only; **train Feb–Apr**, **validate May** (early stopping,
  imbalance choice, thresholds), **test June** (touched once). No random shuffling.
* **Models**: Logistic Regression (`class_weight="balanced"`, scaled + one-hot) as baseline; XGBoost as the tree model.
* **Class imbalance**: for XGBoost I compared no weighting, `sqrt(neg/pos)` and `neg/pos` on validation PR-AUC
  (0.782 / 0.772 / 0.769) and kept **no weighting**. With early stopping and a tuned decision threshold, reweighting
  added nothing and distorted the score scale. I did not use SMOTE, because synthetic interpolated rows break the
  time/velocity structure of the features. The imbalance is handled by the **threshold**, chosen on validation.
* **Decision policy** (two thresholds from validation, frozen for test): score ≥ 0.252 (max-F1) → **decline**;
  0.003–0.252 → **manual review** (band sized to reach 90% validation recall); below → approve.

## 3. Results (June hold-out, `reports/model_results.md`)

| Model | Precision | Recall | F1 | PR-AUC | ROC-AUC | Confusion matrix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic Regression | 0.743 | 0.755 | 0.749 | 0.812 | 0.986 | TN 15,317 · FP 48 · FN 45 · TP 139 |
| **XGBoost (chosen)** | **0.889** | **0.739** | **0.807** | **0.877** | **0.996** | TN 15,348 · FP 17 · FN 48 · TP 136 |

* Bootstrap 95% CI: XGBoost PR-AUC [0.836, 0.913]; XGBoost − LR difference [0.034, 0.100], so the gain is not noise.
* Decline + review together catch **97% of fraud (97% of fraud value)** for ~20 reviews/day.
* Top features: seconds since device's last txn, night, merchant tier, device age, hour.

**Which metric matters most:** **PR-AUC** for comparing models, because with ~1% fraud ROC-AUC looks excellent
even for weak models (both are > 0.98 here), while PR-AUC reflects performance on the rare class. At the
operating point, **recall** (ideally *fraud-amount recall*) is the main business metric: a missed fraud is a direct
loss. It is constrained by **precision**, because every false positive is a declined genuine customer or a manual
review. That is why the threshold is set on validation for an explicit precision/recall trade-off, not left at 0.5.

## 4. Release checks (`src/validate.py`, `reports/release_checks.md`; verdict PASS)

1. **Schema & types**: required columns, datetime parse, numeric/positive amount, 4-digit MCC, allowed category sets, unique `request_id`, MCC↔title consistency.
2. **Missing values & ranges**: missing rate ≤ 2× training + 1pp, amount ≤ 3× training max, share above training p99, daily median amount per service within 3× of training (catches unit errors), unseen-category rate.
3. **Training-serving consistency**: June is replayed row-by-row through an online feature-store implementation (`OnlineFeatureState`) and compared with the batch training features: 15,549 rows × 28 features, **0 mismatches**. Also covered in `tests/`, together with a future-leakage test (features for time *t* are unchanged when later rows are deleted).
4. **Version, evaluation, rollback**: `model_card.json` stores version (`fraud-xgb-v1.0.0`), data hash, windows, features, thresholds, metrics and CIs. Evaluation is reproduced from the saved artifact. Release gate: PR-AUC ≥ 0.6, recall ≥ 0.6, precision ≥ 0.5, and the model must beat the LR baseline. Rollout goes shadow (1–2 weeks) → canary 5–10% → full. **Rollback** to the previous version or the rule engine is a single config flip, triggered by a parity/schema failure, a >1pp approval-rate drop, a review queue >2× capacity, or an SLO breach.

## 5. Drift monitoring on live Jul–Sep (`reports/monitoring_report.md`)

Reference = training period (features) and out-of-sample May–Jun scores (predictions). PSI thresholds:
< 0.10 ok, 0.10–0.25 warn, ≥ 0.25 alert. For KS I report the statistic rather than the p-value, because
with ~15k rows per month every difference is "significant".

| What | Jun (baseline) | Jul | Aug | Sep |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Data**: service_type PSI | 0.000 | 0.013 | 0.049 | **0.117 warn** |
| **Data**: amount PSI / KS (clean rows) | 0 / 0.005 | 0.007 / 0.038 | 0.022 / 0.057 | 0.050 / 0.092 |
| **Data**: validation | pass | pass | pass | **fail: wallet amounts ~100× (paise), 963 rows quarantined** |
| **Prediction**: score PSI | 0.000 | 0.002 | 0.002 | 0.021 |
| **Performance**: recall | 0.739 | 0.726 | **0.522** | **0.307** |
| **Performance**: PR-AUC | 0.877 | 0.865 | **0.657** | **0.420** |
| **Business**: fraud loss (bps of volume) | 12.9 | 18.6 | **72.8** | **170.4** |
| **Business**: approval rate / false declines | 99.0% / 17 | 99.0% / 23 | 98.8% / 32 | 99.1% / 19 |
| **Business**: review queue per day | 19.7 | 18.0 | 21.8 | 20.9 |

**Key lesson:** input and score drift stayed small, yet recall collapsed. The new fraud looks "normal"
(low-risk tier, daytime, UPI, mid amounts), so it does not shift the overall distributions. Label-based
performance monitoring and fraud-loss tracking are therefore essential, and distribution monitoring alone would have missed it.
A segment slice found the cause: frauds at merchants onboarded after go-live in MCC 4829/5816 had **0% recall**.

**Actions taken / recommended**

| Issue | Action |
|---|---|
| Sep amount unit error (validation fail) | **Investigate data quality**: open incident with integration owner, quarantine rows (rules fallback), exclude from metrics and retraining. Do **not** retrain or move thresholds because of it. |
| service_type PSI 0.12, explained by wallet adoption | Document as expected seasonal/product drift and keep monitoring; refresh the reference window at the next retrain. |
| Score drift small, review queue stable | No **threshold** change needed for capacity reasons. |
| Recall / PR-AUC drop in Aug–Sep, fraud loss 13× baseline | Add a stop-gap rule now, **train a challenger**, **shadow test**, promote if it wins. **Roll back** only if the drop were caused by the new release itself, which it was not here. |

Remediation evaluated on clean September data:

| Option | Recall | F1 | PR-AUC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Champion v1.0 as-is | 0.307 | 0.456 | 0.420 |
| Challenger retrained Feb–mid-Aug | 0.351 | 0.498 | 0.527 |
| Champion + stop-gap rule (new merchant, MCC 4829/5816, amount > 2× merchant avg) | 0.784 | 0.844 | 0.813 |
| **Challenger + stop-gap rule** | **0.814** | **0.855** | **0.828** |

Retraining alone helps only a little, because the new pattern has just ~2 weeks of labels. The rule bridges the gap
until enough labels accumulate. In production, label delay (30–90 days for chargebacks) means Aug–Sep
performance would be known late. Early proxies are the fraud-loss trend, analyst review outcomes and
customer disputes.

## Limitations

* Synthetic data: patterns are simplified and cleaner than reality, so absolute metrics are optimistic. The value of this repo is in the pipeline and the checks.
* Labels are assumed complete and immediate in the monitoring demo. Real chargeback delay and label noise are not simulated.
* Review analysts are assumed to catch all fraud routed to review, and fraud loss counts only auto-approved fraud.
* No hyper-parameter search beyond early stopping and the imbalance strategy. No probability calibration, since scores are used only for ranking and thresholds.
* Only one merchant/device graph view; no cross-entity features (e.g. device↔many merchants rings, IP, customer ID).

## Next steps

* Cost-based threshold (₹ fraud loss vs cost of a false decline/review) per segment, not just max-F1.
* Feature store with streaming aggregates, and the same parity test in CI.
* Scheduled monthly challenger training with rolling windows, and automatic shadow comparison.
* Monitoring per segment (new merchants, MCC, service type) with alerts on segment-level recall and fraud loss.
* Calibration (isotonic) if scores feed downstream risk policies; SHAP reason codes for analysts.
